extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers interested in essays, philosophy, self-reflection, and practical advice on retirement/solitude
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and stylistic guidance for composing reflective, personal essays (Montaigne-style) and for choosing a life of retirement/solitude; covers when and how to withdraw, what occupations and pleasures to keep, and how to write authentically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be one's own / espouse nothing but ourselves
rubrics_metrics.description: Break the knot of our obligations and espouse nothing but ourselves; keep the remainder of life for oneself, not so joined and close as not to be forced away without flaying us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: “Since God gives us leisure to order our removal, let us make ready, truss our baggage, take leave betimes of the company, and disentangle ourselves from those violent importunities that engage us elsewhere and separate us from ourselves.” Preserve independence; do not enslave one’s contentment to the power of another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retire when you can no longer add to society
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Tis time to wean ourselves from society when we can no longer add anything to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He who is not in condition to lend must forbid himself to borrow: know when to withdraw rather than persist in public roles you cannot meaningfully serve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Govern yourself with reverence to reason and conscience
rubrics_metrics.description: In retirement, govern yourself with such reverence to reason and conscience that you would be ashamed to make a false step in their presence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: “Let him soothe and caress himself, and above all things be sure to govern himself with reverence to his reason and conscience to that degree as to be ashamed to make a false step in their presence.” Self-rule and inner shame are prerequisites to solitary life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use external goods only as auxiliaries, not foundations
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ accidental and extraneous commodities only insofar as they are pleasant; do not lay your principal foundation on them because they are unstable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: “We are to use these accidental and extraneous commodities, so far as they are pleasant to us, but by no means to lay our principal foundation there; ‘tis no true one; neither nature nor reason allows it so to be.”

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare for misfortunes by anticipating them
rubrics_metrics.description: Anticipate the accidents of fortune and prepare yourself (mentally and practically) for disgrace, sickness, poverty, and death.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne counsels to represent to oneself the ill to come (as in mock-wars at jousts), to keep remedies at hand, and to furnish oneself with medicines or precautions to blunt suffering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose retirement employment neither laborious nor disagreeable
rubrics_metrics.description: Select an occupation for retirement that is neither excessively laborious nor unpleasing; otherwise, retirement is pointless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: “The employment a man should choose for such a life ought neither to be a laborious nor an unpleasing one; otherwise ‘tis to no purpose at all to be retired.” Choose tasks by personal liking and temperament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice moderation in husbandry (avoid servility or negligence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agriculture/husbandry can be servile or negligently stupid; seek a mean between perpetual solicitude and extreme negligence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Husbandry is 'a very servile employment' yet some parts (gardens) are excusable; avoid letting it become your entire anxious preoccupation or, conversely, give it up to chaotic neglect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use retirement to cultivate letters/reputation (but beware ambition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Retirement can be used to study and 'extract from thence something that may be entirely and absolutely thine own' (reputation via writings), yet this aim must be tempered by sincerity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pliny's advice to devote retirement to the study of letters is cited as a legitimate end ('to acquire by his writings an immortal life'), but Montaigne also warns against seeking glory (see separate criterion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ambition and seeking glory in solitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Ambition is contrary to solitude; glory and repose cannot coexist—retirement sought to secure fame is contradictory and disingenuous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retiring for the sake of name or approbation defeats the purpose: 'Quit with other pleasures that which proceeds from the approbation of another man.' Those who retire but pursue fame are merely changing stage, not abandoning public life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ascetic solitude justified only by sincere religious ends
rubrics_metrics.description: Extreme denial and ascetic withdrawal are only rationally founded when they aim at God and the eternal life promised by religion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Devotional solitude, undertaken for the 'sole end of another happily immortal life,' can legitimately turn afflictions to advantage and justify abandoning worldly conveniences; Montaigne contrasts this with philosophical or affectatious self-denial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware over-studiousness: books can harm health
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive book-employment is as painful as any labor and an enemy to health; intellectual pursuits must not be taken to a degree that impairs well-being.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotation from Florio: 'This plodding occupation of bookes is as painfull as any other, and as great an enemie vnto health...' If study damages health or cheerfulness, it is not worth the cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish true pleasures from those mixed with greater pain
rubrics_metrics.description: Beware pleasures that mask or entail greater pain; true and entire pleasures must be distinguished from those that wheedle us only to strangle us later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne uses the image of pleasure concealing its train and warns that if enjoyment leads to headaches or worse, it is not truly desirable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model your retired life by reason and deliberate premeditation
rubrics_metrics.description: When entering retirement, deliberately institute rules of living by reflection; shake off passions that disturb bodily and mental tranquillity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He who retires 'ought to model this new one he enters into by the rules of reason, and to institute and establish it by premeditation and reflection.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Reserve modest activity to avoid dull and stupid laziness
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep enough employment to 'keep us in breath' and to prevent the harms of dull, stupid laziness, but avoid over-engagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retirement should include limited, sustaining activity rather than either continuous labor or complete idleness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select books that amuse or instruct on life and death
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer readings that are pleasant and easy to amuse, or that comfort and instruct on how to regulate life and death.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: “I for my part care for no other books, but either such as are pleasant and easy, to amuse me, or those that comfort and instruct me how to regulate my life and death.”

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt pleasures and conveniences to temperament and age
rubrics_metrics.description: Hold fast to the pleasures still suited to you as years remove others; choose comforts appropriate to your disposition and infirmities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne admits he needs bodily conveniences and that one should 'whet my appetite to those that remain, more suitable to this other reason.' Don't adopt a one-size-fits-all austerity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare yourself morally before withdrawing into solitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Before retiring into yourself, prepare yourself morally: render yourself one before whom you dare not trip and cultivate shame and respect for yourself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: “Retire yourself into yourself, but first prepare yourself there to receive yourself: it were a folly to trust yourself in your own hands, if you cannot govern yourself.” One may fail alone as much as in company.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep exemplars present to guide conduct in solitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Present continually to your imagination virtuous exemplars (Cato, Phocion, Aristides) to correct deviations and keep you content with yourself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imitate and summon the presence of exemplary figures to make faults shameful and to control intentions when alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer substance over ornamental eloquence
rubrics_metrics.description: Reject eloquence that enchants by itself rather than by the things it signifies; prefer matter and action over mere style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: “Away with that eloquence that enchants us with itself, and not with actual things!” Words must serve to illuminate deeds and truth, not to dazzle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be authentic in speech and writing; avoid flattery and falsification
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain a natural, familiar, and honest style; hate flattery, refuse falsification, and speak/write only what you truly believe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne is 'a sworn enemy to all manner of falsification' and dislikes the servile prostitution of flattering expressions. He prefers blunt, heartfelt expression over ceremonious mendacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value spontaneity and first-draft authenticity in writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Write precipitately when prompted; do not over-polish. Those writings that cost the most pains often turn out worst; allow the natural flow of thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: “I always write my letters post-haste... I never transcribe any... Those that cost me the most pains, are the worst; when I once begin to draw it in by head and shoulders, ‘tis a sign that I am not there. I fall too without premeditation or design; the first word begets the second.”

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid encumbering fronts and inscriptions with excessive titles and legends
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not overload book fronts, inscriptions, or superscriptions of letters with long legends of qualities and titles; this is bad taste and often risky.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne declines to add the long litany of titles and legends on writings and letters (especially to officials), finding them cumbersome and error-prone; he finds similar flattery on book-fronts in poor taste.
